And among the most wondrous of the great created things on which the human eye may fall is the sky. For wherever he stands on the earth, he sees half of the sphere that encompasses the earth. When the one looking at it looks reflectively, he sees that the One who created it by His will is unending in His power, His wisdom, and His majesty. For when we are shown some trace of an ancient building of an early people, we marvel at their power to do its like — it indicates to us the strength of their bodies and the loftiness of their ambition in fortifying themselves. If this small look and this slight trace looms so large in our eyes — though it does not exceed our own work except by a little — how much more must we hold in awe the Creator of the earth and the sky and what is between them, without burden, without trouble, without weariness, without fatigue — not from anything, not upon anything, not by means of anything, but by His will and His wish — as it is said: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of His mouth all their host" (Psalms 33:6).

And among the totality of blessings upon the human: whenever you reflect on the traces of wisdom in the created things, you find them — along with their witness to the Creator (exalted be He) for lordship and unity — never separate from an aspect of benefit and an intent for welfare for the human being, save that some of them are manifest and some hidden. Among these are light and darkness: the benefits of light are evident and manifest, not hidden. As for darkness, its benefits are hidden — because of people's loneliness within it, and the cutting-off of their works and movements at its falling. Yet were it not for the darkness of night, the bodies of most animals would have been cut off by the continuity of their labor, the persistence of their work, and the length of their motion. By night, one part of time is parsed off from another; by it the unknown stretches of time and the length and shortness of terms are determined. And were the state always upon one form, there would have been no Law containing in itself time — like the Sabbath, the festival, the fast — and there would be no promise among people up to a fixed time; and ignorance of most of the things contained in time; and the digestion of food in the stomach of any animal would not have been complete.

Since the human had need of light by night to do some of his works in it — and to be cheered by it in his sickness — God compensated him with the light of fire, to employ it by night whenever he wills and extinguish it whenever he wills.

וּמִמַּעֲלוֹת הַשֵּׂכֶל שֶׁבּוֹ יַשִּׂיג הָאָדָם כָּל מֻשָּׂגָיו הַמּוּחָשִׁים וְהַמֻּשְׂכָּלִים.

וּבוֹ יִרְאֶה מָה שֶׁנֶּעֱלַם מֵחוּשָׁיו הַגַּשְׁמִיִּים מִן הַנִּרְאוֹת כִּנְסִיעַת הַצֵּל וּמַעֲשֵׂה הַטִּפָּה הָאַחַת מִן הַמַּיִם בְּצוּר הַחַלָּמִישׁ.

וּבוֹ יַבְדִּיל בֵּין הָאֱמֶת וְהַשֶּׁקֶר וּבֵין הַיָּתֵר וְהֶחָסֵר וְהַטּוֹב וְהָרַע וְהַמְּשֻׁבָּח וְהַמְּגֻנֶּה וּבֵין הָרָאוּי וְהָאֶפְשָׁר וְהַנִּמְנָע.

וּבוֹ יַעֲבִיד שְׁאָר מִינֵי חַיִּים בְּתוֹעֲלוֹתָיו וַהֲנָאוֹתָיו וְיַכִּיר מְקוֹמוֹת הַכּוֹכָבִים וְיַעֲמֹד עַל מֶרְחַקֵּיהֶם וּתְנוּעוֹת גַּלְגַּלֵּיהֶם וְיָבִין הָעֲרָכִים וְהַהֶקֵּשׁוֹת שֶׁבְּחָכְמַת הַשִּׁעוּר וְצוּרוֹת הַמּוֹפֵת אֲשֶׁר בְּחָכְמַת הַדִּבּוּר וּשְׁאָר הַחָכְמוֹת וְהַמְּלָאכוֹת שֶׁיֶּאֱרַךְ זִכְרָם.
